10.1002_aenm.202506548: Electrocatalytic technology represents a pivotal pathway for converting low‐value feedstocks into high‐value products, though its practical implementation continues to face fundamental challenges such as sluggish reaction kinetics and high energy barriers. These limitations are increasingly being overcome through multi‐active site (MAS) architectures, which utilize synergistic effects to facilitate multi‐electron transfer processes and establish a new paradigm in catalyst design. This review systematically explores rational design and engineering strategies for MAS structures, covering approaches such as heterostructure construction, dual‐atom site modulation, defect engineering, alloying, and cascade reaction systems, all aimed at improving overall electrocatalytic performance. We further analyze the intrinsic mechanisms responsible for performance breakthroughs in MAS architectures, including their ability to decouple reaction steps, optimize intermediate adsorption, enable electron–proton co‐transfer, and suppress competing side reactions. By integrating advanced characterization techniques with theoretical simulations, this work also reveals key cooperative mechanisms and dynamic reaction pathways, establishes a foundational framework for catalyst refinement, and details applications of multi‐component active sites across major catalytic reactions. Finally, we outline persistent challenges and propose future research directions, offering a systematic theoretical basis for the development of next‐generation electrocatalysts for sustainable energy systems.
10.1002_cey2.70177: Transition metal sulfides demonstrate remarkable theoretical specific capacities, making them highly desirable anode materials for sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs). Nevertheless, low electrical conductivity and restacking seriously limit their electrochemical activity, resulting in suboptimal specific capacity and cycling stability. Herein, it is demonstrated that self‐doped PVP‐VS 4 /Ti 3 C 2 T x presents multidirectional open conductive channels and sufficient vacancies for reversible and fast Na + insertion/extraction. The PVP‐VS 4 /Ti 3 C 2 T x exhibits excellent rate performance (80.5% capacity retention from 0.1 to 10.0 A g −1 ) and superior cycling stability (711 mAh g −1 after 1000 cycles at 5 A g −1 and 518 mAh g −1 after 600 cycles at 10 A g −1 ). The sodium storage mechanism of the PVP‐VS 4 /Ti 3 C 2 T x anode was elucidated through in situ XRD, ex situ HRTEM, and ex situ XPS analyses. The DFT calculation demonstrates that the interfacial structure of PVP‐VS 4 /Ti 3 C 2 T x significantly enhances the electronic conductivity as an anode. Impressively, the assembled NaFePO 4 //PVP‐VS 4 /Ti 3 C 2 T x full cell retained 87.2% of capacity after 500 cycles at 0.5 C, and still allowed the LEDs to remain lighted after cycling. This study offers a fresh perspective on improving the electrochemical performance of vanadium tetrasulfide through Ti 3 C 2 T x as a conductive base to support PVP‐induced VS 4 .
10.1021_acs.accounts.6c00727: Conspectus Sustainable electrochemical energy conversion relies on functional materials that enable efficient transport while withstanding demanding operating environments. Anion-exchange membrane fuel cells (AEMFCs) and anion-exchange membrane water electrolyzers (AEMWEs) are attractive platforms because their alkaline environments enable the use of nonprecious-metal catalysts and hydrocarbon-based polymer electrolytes. Anion-exchange polyelectrolytes (APEs) are central to these devices, serving as both free-standing anion-exchange membranes (AEMs) and catalyst-layer anion-exchange ionomers (AEIs). Although AEMs and AEIs share related polymer chemistries, their distinct operating environments and functional roles impose different requirements on molecular design. Our work on AEMs has focused on the coupled requirements of hydroxide transport, chemical stability, dimensional control, and mechanical durability. We first examined how polymer architecture and chain packing affect the formation of ion-conducting domains and confined transport environments. As conductivity improved, chemical degradation and mechanically induced failure became increasingly relevant, leading us to investigate cation stability, local electronic environments, dimensional constraints, and molecular-level stress dissipation. These studies showed that AEMs cannot be optimized on the basis of a single performance metric but instead require the coordinated regulation of ion transport, molecular stability, and mechanical response. We also extended this work to kilogram-scale polymer synthesis and continuous roll-to-roll membrane fabrication, where synthetic reproducibility and processing compatibility become additional constraints on molecular design. The requirements change when APEs are used as catalyst-layer ionomers. AEIs form nanometer-scale films around catalyst particles and must provide local hydroxide conduction while allowing water and gas transport, maintaining catalyst accessibility, and contributing to interfacial integrity. Our studies on AEIs have therefore examined multiphase transport, catalyst-ionomer interactions, interfacial adhesion, ionomer distribution, and catalyst-layer structure. Fluorinated and porous ionomers were used to regulate oxygen transport and gas-bubble removal, while conformational and interfacial design was used to reduce unfavorable catalyst-ionomer interactions. Further control of adhesion, ionomer-film organization, and catalyst immobilization showed that catalyst-layer performance also depends strongly on how the ionomer is distributed and organized during electrode formation. The studies discussed in this Account suggest that APE molecular design should be matched to the specific operating environment and functional role of the polymer within the membrane-electrode assembly. For AEMs, this includes balancing transport, durability, and manufacturability; for AEIs, it additionally requires control of local transport, catalyst interactions, and catalyst-layer organization.
10.1021_acsenergylett.6c01583: Solid-state sodium metal batteries suffer from interfacial instability due to poor physical contact, uneven ion flux, and uncontrolled dendrite growth. Herein, a self-assembled homogeneous interphase composed of sodiophilic Na15Sn4 and electronically insulating Na2S is proposed to homogenize Na+ deposition, suppress dendrite growth, and ensure interfacial bonding stability. Ex situ SEM analysis after cycling reveals a crack-free and dendrite-free morphology, contrasting sharply with the catastrophic failure observed for bare Na. This composite anode endows the Na15Sn4/Na2S@Na//NFM full cell with ultrafast charging capability and outstanding wide-temperature performance (–30 °C ∼ 60 °C). The full cell retains 78.6% of its capacity after 500 cycles at 2 C. A pouch cell delivers 408 Wh kg–1 and passes destructive abuse tests (bending, nailing, shearing, and cutting), proving its practical viability. This work presents an interface engineering that balances ionic conductivity, mechanical strength, and chemical compatibility. It offers a versatile strategy for stabilizing reactive metal anodes beyond Na.
10.1038_s41467-026-75106-5: Skeletal muscle operates through a mechanism in which calcium ions act as a trigger at low electric potentials, followed by contraction powered by adenosine triphosphate hydrolysis. Inspired by this process, we have developed an electrochemical artificial muscle with low-voltage redox triggering and spontaneous contraction. Triggering is achieved by electrochemically charging the muscles at voltages below 0.4 V, which enables I3⁻ injection and subsequent oxidation to I2. Spontaneous muscle contraction then occurs via the reaction I2 + I⁻ → I3⁻, analogous to the role of adenosine triphosphate in skeletal muscle contraction, yet fundamentally distinct from conventional electrochemical artificial muscles. Following this mechanism, pristine carbon nanotube yarn muscles and carbon nanotube yarn muscles modified by quaternary ammonium cations generated contractile strokes of 5.2% and 15.5%, respectively. Moreover, the contracted state can be stably maintained without electrical energy input, and full recovery to the original length is achieved by applying a reverse voltage. Such mechanisms present a promising strategy for the development of energy-efficient artificial muscles. An electrochemical artificial muscle that features low-voltage triggering and spontaneous contraction was developed by utilizing triiodide/iodide redox reactions, mimicking skeletal muscle contraction.
